title: Question 9
stem:
Nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (NMRI) is used to obtain diagnostic information about internal body structures.

State, during the use of NMRI, the function of:

parts.label: (a)

markscheme_points.text: precession is about direction of m
frequency of precession depends or frequency of precession is in radi

hints: Hint 1: Start by picturing the hydrogen nuclei in the body as tiny spinning magnets. What would a very strong, steady magnetic field do to their orientation and motion?
Hint 2: Think of a spinning top wobbling around the vertical. The nuclei do something similar around the field direction - what do we call this wobble and what controls how fast it happens?
Hint 3: Recall why NMRI needs radio waves. How must the wobbling rate relate to the frequency of the applied RF pulse for energy to be absorbed?
parts.proper_answer: The large constant field causes the hydrogen nuclei (protons) to precess about the direction of the field. The precession (Larmor) frequency is proportional to the magnetic flux density and lies in the radio-frequency range, so the nuclei can be made to resonate by an RF pulse.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Making Nuclei Precess**
Think of each hydrogen nucleus in the body as a tiny spinning bar magnet. Without an external field their magnetic axes point randomly. When you put the patient inside a large uniform field $B_0$, the axes line up roughly with or against $B_0$ but, because they are spinning, they do not sit still. They wobble in a cone around the field direction. This wobbling is called precession.

Step 2: **Setting the Larmor Frequency**
The rate of this wobble is very regular and is called the Larmor frequency $f$. It is directly proportional to the strength of the large field, so a large $B_0$ gives a well-defined high frequency. For the fields used in NMRI, typically about $1\text{ T}$, this frequency falls in the radio-frequency part of the spectrum, e.g. about $42\text{ MHz}$.

Step 3: **Preparing for Resonance**
That is the whole purpose of the big magnet. It creates a uniform population of nuclei all precessing together at a known radio frequency. A pulse of radio waves at exactly that same frequency can then be absorbed to flip the nuclei to a higher energy state (resonance), which is the starting point for imaging.

hints: Hint 1: You have just seen that precession frequency depends on the strength of the field. If the field is made slightly stronger at one end of the body than the other, what will happen to the frequency from point to point?
Hint 2: Only nuclei whose precession frequency exactly matches the RF pulse will resonate. How does that let you pick out where in the body the signal is coming from?
parts.proper_answer: The non-uniform (gradient) field is superimposed on the large constant field so that the total field, and hence the Larmor frequency, varies with position. Only nuclei in the region where the frequency matches the RF resonate, allowing the position of the signal to be located and the region scanned to be changed to build up an image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Making Frequency Depend on Position**
The large magnet alone gives the same $B_0$ and the same Larmor frequency everywhere, so you could not tell one part of the body from another. Adding a small gradient field means $B$ is now slightly different at different positions. Since $f$ is proportional to $B$, the precession frequency now codes for position.

Step 2: **Locating and Selecting Slices**
Resonance only happens where $f$ equals the frequency of the RF pulse. So the detector knows the detected radio emission must have come from that particular position or slice. By varying the gradient, you sweep the resonant condition through different regions and build up a full 3D map of hydrogen concentration.
